title: Does an antibody Fab need a specialist model?
content: Antibody Fabs can be significant drug candidates, and their small, multi-chain structure presents a challenge in protein engineering. We tried out two approaches, with some surprising results. Lead optimization, the iterative refinement of candidate molecules to enhance their functional profiles, remains the longest and most expensive pre-clinical step in protein engineering. A promising lead rarely possesses all the properties required for practical application, and this is equally true whether you’re developing an antibody or peptide to become a drug, or an enzyme as a crop, food ingredient, or consumer product. In all cases, simultaneous improvement/optimization of multiple traits is necessary. But these often come with trade-offs: For therapeutic antibodies, this might mean that your efforts to increase affinity come at the cost of expression or thermostability. Before protein engineering with machine learning, finding a candidate that matched all necessary properties was long, tedious, and usually disappointing. Optimization or other preclinical work would typically consume 12-36 months and cost $5M-$15M per candidate , with only 1 in 14.6 candidates reaching successful product launch . The standard approach follows design-build-test-learn cycles: Design variants of the candidate molecule, build and test them in the lab, then take what worked to the next round, tweaking the winners to try and arrive at the next property in the profile. Protein language models have accelerated this process by learning from evolutionary patterns at a scale unfathomable by humans to guide variant design . But not all models are created equal, and the question of whether to use a specialized (e.g. antibody-specific) model or a general one isn’t always obvious. Experimenting with different setups and questioning assumptions is a big part of what we do at Cradle’s ML hub in Zurich, so we thought it would be instructive to put that question to the test. Fabs are highly relevant in drug discovery, having been developed into treatments for common conditions including age-related macular degeneration and rheumatoid arthritis, and as both coagulants and anticoagulants for use during surgery. Ranibizumab, certolizumab pegol, abciximab and idarucizumab are all Fabs. They are also hard to engineer: Two separate protein chains that have to work as one unit, which is a structure a general-purpose ML model wasn’t made for. If a specialist model is needed to optimize this class well, any team working on this class is constrained to whatever specialist models happen to exist. We ran a 65-million-parameter antibody-specific model and a 650-million-parameter general protein model through the identical Cradle fine-tuning pipeline, on the same molecule, with the same four properties improved at once, across nearly 400 lab-measured designs. The result? Neither architecture won. What determined performance was the fine-tuning, which is the part we control and the part that transfers to a customer’s molecule regardless of its format. Cradle tested whether a machine learning model built specifically for antibodies designs better drug candidates than a general-purpose protein model when compared inside our multi-step finetuning pipeline. The starting molecule was C102, an antibody fragment (a “Fab”) made of two protein chains that binds the SARS-CoV-2 virus (specifically, part of the famous “spike” protein). The antibody-specific model was built to read both chains together, while the general model reads both chains as one combined protein. The models also differ in size. The general model has about 650 million parameters and the antibody-specific model about 65 million. (A model's parameters are the internal numbers it adjusts as it learns.) Both models were given the same extra training on this antibody and ran through two rounds of design and lab testing. The goal was to improve four properties at once: binding to the original virus, binding to a mutated version of it, thermostability, and the amount of protein produced. Neither model won outright. The general model designed the tightest binder, which bound the original virus 20.3 times more strongly than the starting antibody. The antibody-specific model designed the most heat-stable variant, which melts 12.5 °C higher. Of the 37 designs where no other design was better on all four properties, 20 came from the antibody-specific model and 17 from the general model, a gap small enough to be due to chance. We conclude that, on this task, the extra training mattered more than which model the team started with. This test ran on a single antibody, and the two models differ in size, design, and original training data, so the result cannot be credited to any single factor. Our takeaway: A model's ability heavily depends on fine-tuning and the context it is being used in. Just because a model is purpose-built for a job doesn't make it better for your job.
